paragraphs: Understanding a video involves recognizing objects and following how their states change. This paper introduces the Kalman variational auto-encoder, which learns those aspects through two separate latent representations. One comes from a recognition model and represents an object; the other describes the state underlying its dynamics. The framework learns from sequential data without supervision.

The separation supports reasoning about change in a compact internal space instead of working directly with every pixel of every frame. The model can imagine how a scene evolves and fill in missing observations without generating a complete, high-dimensional image at each intermediate time step. This makes the learned dynamics useful beyond simply reconstructing individual video frames.

The authors train the framework end to end using videos of several simulated physical systems. They report better performance than competing methods on generation and missing-data imputation. These findings support the usefulness of separating recognition from dynamics for the tested sequential learning tasks.
neurips-2017-a-disentangled-recognition-.tldr: The Kalman variational auto-encoder separates object representations from dynamics to generate sequences and fill missing observations in latent space.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels can be noisy, so assessing the people who provide them is a central statistical problem. This paper studies how accurately worker reliability can be estimated from their labels. It first establishes a lower bound on minimax estimation error: a limit on the best worst-case accuracy that any estimation procedure can achieve in the problem considered.

The authors then introduce Triangular Estimation, or TE, and prove that it matches this lower bound. This establishes minimax optimality, connecting an achievable algorithm to the fundamental estimation limit. The claim concerns worst-case estimation error in the studied setting, rather than saying that TE must outperform every alternative on each individual dataset.

TE also has practical computational properties: it has low complexity, avoids an iterative procedure, and can operate as workers supply labels in real time. The paper evaluates it alongside other leading algorithms on synthetic and real-world data. Together, the results connect statistical optimality with an implementation suitable for streaming crowdsourcing workflows.
neurips-2017-a-minimax-optimal-algorithm.tldr: Triangular Estimation estimates worker reliability with low computational complexity and provably optimal worst-case error.

paragraphs: Estimating relationships among thousands of variables can be computationally demanding and difficult to interpret. This paper addresses that problem for l1-regularized Ising models by identifying the block structure of a solution. The blocks group variables into separate parts of the fitted relationship structure, making moderate-size clusters available for closer examination.

The main contribution is a simple screening rule with a closed-form expression. For any specified regularization parameters, its condition is both necessary and sufficient to recover the solution's block structure exactly. This is stronger than a heuristic for finding plausible clusters: the rule characterizes the actual block structure of the regularized solution.

When the solution is sufficiently sparse, the screening rule can work with different optimization procedures to make estimation efficient in practice. This is particularly useful for exploratory analysis focused on a small set of interpretable relationships within a much larger dataset. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate computational efficiency and analytical insights from using the rule.
neurips-2017-a-screening-rule-for-l1-reg.tldr: A closed-form screening rule exactly identifies blocks in l1-regularized Ising solutions and can accelerate estimation when sufficient sparsity is present.

paragraphs: This paper studies parallel sampling from a Gaussian distribution with many dimensions. It proposes a generalized Gibbs sampler that produces samples approximately following the desired distribution. The approximation is part of the method's design: the sampler targets a distribution that differs from the original Gaussian rather than claiming to sample it exactly.

The distinguishing feature is a single parameter that controls a tradeoff between bias and variance. Bias captures systematic discrepancy associated with the approximation, while variance concerns variability in sampling-based results. Having one adjustable control makes the compromise explicit, allowing the method to balance these two sources of error instead of accepting a fixed approximation.

The authors compare their approach empirically with Hogwild-type algorithms, which also target an approximation to the original distribution. They report that their method is flexible and performs well in those comparisons. The contribution is therefore an adjustable approach to approximate high-dimensional Gaussian sampling, supported by experimental evidence rather than a claim of universally superior sampling accuracy.
neurips-2017-clone-mcmc-parallel-high-di.tldr: Clone MCMC provides approximate Gaussian Gibbs sampling with a single parameter for trading bias against variance.

paragraphs: When observations are spread across servers, learning their underlying distribution also requires communication. This paper asks how many bits the servers must send to a central referee to estimate a discrete distribution accurately. It studies estimation error under both l1 and l2 measures and establishes upper and lower communication bounds across several settings.

One result identifies a strong obstacle: for an unstructured distribution with just one sample per server, even arbitrary interaction through public messages essentially requires communicating the entire sample. In this setting, an elaborate communication protocol cannot avoid the basic cost of transmitting the observed data.

Structure changes what is achievable. For distributions such as k-histograms and monotone distributions, the authors design algorithms that communicate substantially less than naive approaches. They obtain matching upper and lower bounds in several regimes, and their algorithms run in near-linear time while tolerating model misspecification. The findings explain how distributional structure can enable communication savings that are unavailable in the unstructured setting.
neurips-2017-communication-efficient-dis.tldr: The paper establishes communication limits for distributed distribution estimation and shows how structured distributions permit substantial savings.

paragraphs: Embedding models learn representations by predicting an observation from its context. In language, the observation can be a word and the context other words; in recommendation, both can be items. This paper examines a modeling choice within that setup: whether every available context element should participate in predicting the target.

The authors show that using the entire context is not optimal and instead learn a subset on which to condition the target probability. They use amortized variational inference to choose that subset automatically. Context selection therefore becomes part of the learned probabilistic model, connecting the representation task with the decision about which surrounding observations to use.

Compared with standard embedding models, the proposed method improves both predictions and embedding quality. These findings indicate that selecting context can benefit the representations themselves, as well as the immediate prediction task. The contribution is a way to learn what information to condition on within the embedding framework, rather than treating the supplied context as uniformly useful.
neurips-2017-context-selection-for-embed.tldr: Learning which context elements to use improves predictions and representation quality over standard embedding models.

paragraphs: This paper develops an optimization method for convex regularized empirical risk minimization, where training balances fit to observed data with a regularization term. Its focus is mini-batch training. Mini-batches stabilize gradient estimates and support parallel computation, but an optimization method must use them efficiently to turn those advantages into faster progress.

The proposed stochastic gradient method combines a new double-acceleration technique with variance reduction. The theoretical analysis shows improved mini-batch efficiency relative to previous accelerated stochastic methods. With a training set of size n, the method essentially needs batches of size square root of n to achieve optimal iteration complexity for both strongly convex and non-strongly convex objectives.

The authors also analyze operation without mini-batches, obtaining the best known convergence rate for both objective classes. These results concern how efficiently optimization approaches a solution, with separate guarantees covering the two convex settings. The contribution is a combination of acceleration and variance reduction that strengthens the theoretical case for efficient mini-batch optimization.
neurips-2017-doubly-accelerated-stochast.tldr: Double acceleration and variance reduction improve convex optimization efficiency, attaining optimal iteration complexity with essentially square-root-sized mini-batches.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks train models and discriminators through competition. This paper examines that arrangement through the Turing test, identifying features that define such learning from that perspective. It uses those features to outline a broader family of methods called Turing Learning, extending the possibilities for how models and discriminators interact.

The central extension explored here gives discriminators an active role in obtaining evidence. Instead of only judging supplied samples, they can interact with the processes producing them. The discriminator becomes an interrogator that influences the conditions under which observations arise, bringing the learning setup closer to the interactive character of the Turing test.

Two case studies test the idea. A computer learns an agent's behavior while controlling its environment, and a robot learns its own sensor configuration while controlling its movements. Allowing interrogation improves model accuracy in these studies. The results support active interaction as a useful generalization of adversarial learning in the examined behavior and sensor-learning settings.
neurips-2017-generalizing-gans-a-turing-.tldr: Turing Learning extends adversarial learning by letting discriminators actively interrogate data-producing processes, improving accuracy in two case studies.

paragraphs: GAN-based semi-supervised learning had shown strong classification results, but the generator's role in those results was unclear. This paper asks how jointly training a generator helps the discriminator classify data, and why strong classification and high-quality generation can be difficult to obtain together. It treats these as related questions about the training objective.

The theoretical analysis shows that, given the discriminator objective under consideration, good semi-supervised learning requires a generator that is bad at the generative task. The authors also define a preferred generator for that setting. The condition on the objective matters: the result identifies a tension within the analyzed formulation rather than a universal incompatibility between generation and classification.

Using this analysis, the authors develop a new formulation that substantially improves on feature matching GANs in their experiments. It achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark datasets. The findings show how understanding the generator's role in classification can guide a more effective semi-supervised learning method.
neurips-2017-good-semi-supervised-learni.tldr: Under the analyzed discriminator objective, effective semi-supervised classification requires a poor generator, motivating a formulation with stronger benchmark results.

paragraphs: Tracking an arbitrary object through video is difficult when clutter contains many distracting visual features. Because the target's class is not fixed in advance, a target-specific discriminative model cannot simply be prepared beforehand. This paper develops a recurrent tracking model with hierarchical attention, inspired by spatial attention and separate processing of location and identity in human vision.

The attention hierarchy narrows the visual information in stages. Its first layer selects a region containing the target, removing most of the background from consideration. Later layers focus on features specific to the tracked object. These stages connect the question of where to look with the question of which visual details identify the target.

The complete framework is differentiable and trainable from data using gradient methods. The authors add tracking-related auxiliary tasks to the loss to improve training convergence. They evaluate the model on pedestrian tracking in KTH and on the more difficult KITTI tracking dataset, examining the approach across two video-tracking settings.
neurips-2017-hierarchical-attentive-recu.tldr: A recurrent tracker uses layered attention to select the target region and then focus on object-specific visual features.

paragraphs: A curve can carry uncertainty as well as a central trajectory. This paper studies populations of curves represented by non-degenerate Gaussian processes, so that variation within each curve representation remains part of the analysis. The aim is to compare and summarize uncertain functions without reducing each one to a single fixed curve.

The authors use the 2-Wasserstein metric to define a geometry for Gaussian processes with L2 mean and covariance functions over compact index spaces. Within that setting, they prove that a population has a unique barycenter, an average defined through the metric. This gives a mathematically well-defined way to summarize a collection of uncertain curves.

They also prove convergence of distances and barycenters computed using finite-dimensional counterparts. Those results justify practical calculations that approximate the underlying function-valued objects. Experiments on Gaussian-process datasets describing brain connectivity and climate development demonstrate the framework, linking its mathematical treatment of uncertainty to population analysis in two application areas.
neurips-2017-learning-from-uncertain-cur.tldr: A Wasserstein geometry enables comparison and averaging of uncertain curves represented as Gaussian processes, with guarantees supporting finite-dimensional computation.

paragraphs: Streaming learning often assumes that the same features remain available over time. This paper considers a different situation: old features disappear and new ones arrive, as can happen when sensors are replaced. The proposed Feature Evolvable Streaming Learning framework seeks to preserve useful information from vanished features while learning from those currently available.

The method attempts to recover the old features and trains separate models using recovered and current features. It then offers two ways to use their predictions. One combines the models' outputs; the other dynamically selects a single prediction. These approaches let information associated with earlier features continue contributing after the observed feature set changes.

For the combination method, the authors theoretically show that assistance from old features can improve performance on new features. For dynamic selection, they establish a stronger performance guarantee when the best model changes over time. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the proposal's effectiveness, demonstrating the value of carrying information across feature transitions.
neurips-2017-learning-with-feature-evolv.tldr: Recovering vanished features and combining their predictions with current-feature models improves learning in streams whose feature sets change.

paragraphs: A Gaussian process model may need to respect known linear constraints on the function it represents. This paper incorporates those constraints by modifying the covariance function, which describes how function values vary together. The goal is to make the known relationships part of the model's structure, so they hold throughout its predictions and samples.

The construction represents the target function as a transformation of an underlying function. By designing that transformation around the constraints, the authors ensure that every sampled function and every prediction satisfies them. The guarantee therefore applies to the model's possible outputs, rather than only to agreement with constraints at particular observed examples.

The paper also provides a constructive procedure for designing the transformation operator. This turns the modeling principle into a way to build constrained Gaussian processes for a given problem. Illustrations on simulated and real data demonstrate the resulting approach. The contribution connects explicit prior knowledge about linear relationships with a covariance construction that enforces those relationships by design.
neurips-2017-linearly-constrained-gaussi.tldr: A transformed Gaussian process covariance guarantees that all samples and predictions satisfy specified linear constraints.

paragraphs: This paper introduces the Vector Quantised-Variational AutoEncoder, or VQ-VAE, for learning useful representations without supervision. Its encoder produces discrete codes instead of continuous latent values, using ideas from vector quantisation. The model also learns its prior, the distribution describing latent codes, rather than keeping that distribution fixed.

A central motivation is posterior collapse: a powerful autoregressive decoder can ignore the latent representation in a conventional VAE. The authors report that their vector-quantisation approach circumvents this problem. This matters because a representation has limited value if the generative model learns to produce outputs without making use of it.

Combined with an autoregressive prior, the learned representations support high-quality generation of images, videos, and speech. The paper also reports high-quality speaker conversion and unsupervised phoneme learning. These applications provide evidence that the discrete codes capture useful information across different kinds of data, connecting the representation-learning design to both generation and speech-related tasks.
neurips-2017-neural-discrete-representat.tldr: VQ-VAE learns discrete latent codes and a learned prior, avoiding posterior collapse and supporting image, video, and speech applications.

paragraphs: Frank-Wolfe is a method for constrained convex optimization. This paper gives it another interpretation: its optimization process can be viewed as computing an equilibrium of a particular convex-concave zero-sum game. The equilibrium is a saddle point, connecting the search for an optimization solution with the interaction between opposing objectives.

The connection relies on no-regret online learning. These learning procedures generate the sequence of iterates, while their vanishing regret also supplies a convergence argument. In this way, the same online-learning machinery explains both how the optimization updates arise and why they approach a solution in the studied formulation.

The authors emphasize that the interpretation is modular. It provides a framework from which both existing and new algorithms can emerge, rather than only a new explanation of one established method. They explore several resulting methods and report experiments demonstrating correctness and efficiency. The contribution links optimization and equilibrium computation in a form that supports algorithm design as well as analysis.
neurips-2017-on-frank-wolfe-and-equilibr.tldr: Frank-Wolfe can be understood as no-regret learning toward a game equilibrium, yielding convergence proofs and a modular route to algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper considers repeatedly solving related dynamic programming problems as the environment changes. Its motivating example is choosing a binary search tree before learning how frequently its keys and gaps will be searched. Each trial produces a search cost, and the frequencies may change before the next trial.

The learning objective is to keep total cost close to that of the best single tree selected afterward with knowledge of every trial. This hindsight comparison evaluates whether the learner adapts its choices effectively despite having to act before seeing the current frequencies. The computational challenge is that the possible trees form an exponentially large set.

The authors develop a general methodology for a broad class of dynamic programming algorithms, using their problem structure to support online learning over large collections of combinatorial objects. The framework extends methods such as Hedge and Component Hedge to more kinds of objects than previously possible. Its contribution is a bridge between dynamic programming structure and repeated decision-making under changing costs.
neurips-2017-online-dynamic-programming-.tldr: The framework extends online learning to dynamic programming problems with exponentially many choices, including search trees under changing access frequencies.

paragraphs: Anticipating a visual scene requires understanding both what will appear and how it will move. This paper develops a model that predicts future scene parsing and motion together. Scene parsing provides dense semantic labels describing objects and their locations, while motion prediction describes how those objects move in future frames.

The model takes preceding video frames and their scene-parsing results as input. It can produce predictions for arbitrary future time steps, and joint learning uses the complementary relationship between the two tasks. The central idea is that anticipating scene structure and anticipating movement can inform one another within a shared predictive model.

On Cityscapes, the authors report significantly better parsing and motion predictions than established baselines, supporting the benefit of their joint approach in that evaluation. They also demonstrate vehicle steering-angle prediction, providing additional evidence that the model learns underlying latent parameters useful beyond the two main outputs. These results connect future visual understanding with information relevant to vehicle behavior.
neurips-2017-predicting-scene-parsing-an.tldr: Jointly forecasting future semantic scene structure and motion improves both tasks on Cityscapes and also supports steering-angle prediction.

paragraphs: High-level rules describe common principles across examples, but generating examples from rules raises a different problem. This paper studies rule realization in discrete input spaces: constructing probability distributions over samples that follow supplied rules. It also asks which rules should be realized when the initial collection contains inconsistencies.

Rule selection and realization are formulated as connected parts of one symmetric bi-convex optimization problem. This couples the choice of reasonable rules with the construction of distributions that express them. The formulation makes compromise part of the task, addressing situations where accepting every proposed rule would not produce a consistent set of requirements.

The authors derive an efficient algorithm intended to operate at large scale. Music composition rules serve as the main example, and demonstrations cover both generating music and interpreting or understanding it. These applications illustrate the two directions of the framework: realizing principles through examples and using those principles to analyze examples. The contribution brings both directions into a shared probabilistic formulation.
neurips-2017-probabilistic-rule-realizat.tldr: A joint probabilistic formulation selects compatible rules and generates distributions that realize them, with applications to music composition and analysis.

paragraphs: Learning a control policy through experimentation can expose a physical system to harmful actions. This paper incorporates safety directly into model-based reinforcement learning, defining safety through stability guarantees. It extends Lyapunov stability verification to use statistical models of system dynamics and obtain control policies accompanied by provable stability certificates.

The method also addresses how to gather more information safely. Under additional regularity assumptions expressed through a Gaussian process prior, the authors prove that data can be collected safely and effectively to improve the dynamics model. Better knowledge can then improve control performance and expand the region of states certified as safe.

The experiments optimize a neural network policy for a simulated inverted pendulum without the pendulum falling during learning. This demonstrates the approach in a concrete control task. The theoretical guarantees retain their stated assumptions, and the paper's safety concept is stability: the contribution connects policy improvement and exploration to an explicit control-theoretic certificate.
neurips-2017-safe-model-based-reinforcem.tldr: A model-based reinforcement learning method uses stability certificates to improve control and, under stated assumptions, safely expand the certified region.

paragraphs: Neural networks commonly learn a target function from examples of its inputs and outputs. Sometimes its derivatives are available too, describing how outputs change as inputs change. This paper introduces Sobolev Training, which uses both target values and target derivatives during training, incorporating information that ordinary value-matching training may ignore.

Matching derivatives teaches the network about the target function's local behavior as well as its output at particular inputs. This situation arises naturally when the target is another neural network, as in compression or distillation. The additional training signal can improve approximation quality, data efficiency, and generalization by encoding more information about the function being learned.

The authors provide theoretical justification and empirical evidence across three domains: regression on classical optimization datasets, distillation of Atari-playing policies, and large-scale synthetic-gradient applications. In all three, adding derivative targets yields higher accuracy and stronger generalization. The findings support using available derivative information as an additional source of supervision for function approximation.
neurips-2017-sobolev-training-for-neural.tldr: Sobolev Training matches target derivatives as well as outputs, improving accuracy and generalization across three tested domains.

paragraphs: A useful representation of a molecule should reflect properties that remain unchanged when the molecule is translated or rotated. This paper introduces solid harmonic wavelet scattering, a representation for two- and three-dimensional signals that is invariant to rigid motion and stable under deformation. It is designed for regression and classification.

The construction combines solid harmonic functions with Gaussian windows at multiple scales to form wavelets. Cascading wavelet transforms with a complex-modulus nonlinearity produces invariant scattering coefficients. These coefficients describe signals while respecting the stated transformation properties, providing inputs for prediction that do not depend on an arbitrary rigid placement of the signal.

The authors apply the representation to molecular electronic densities to estimate quantum molecular energies, which share the relevant invariance and stability properties. Multilinear regression using the scattering coefficients achieves results close to the state of the art on small and large organic-molecule databases. The findings support pairing a carefully structured representation with a comparatively simple regression model.
neurips-2017-solid-harmonic-wavelet-scat.tldr: Rigid-motion-invariant wavelet scattering descriptors support near-state-of-the-art molecular energy prediction using multilinear regression.

paragraphs: EEG and local field potential recordings can contain large amounts of data while offering few labels for training. Scientific analysis also needs understandable features. This paper addresses both concerns with a convolutional network whose parameterized filters are guided by neuroscience and learn frequency bands relevant to synchrony between electrodes.

Here, synchrony includes frequency-specific correlations in signal power and phase. Targeting those relationships produces an expressive network with only a few hundred parameters, making it applicable to smaller datasets while retaining interpretable features. The authors report competitive, often state-of-the-art predictive performance in their empirical evaluations.

A Gaussian process adapter allows datasets with different electrode layouts to be analyzed jointly. This supports pooling information across recordings to address overfitting and improve generalizability. The framework also tracks neural dynamics in children participating in an autism spectrum disorder clinical trial. That application demonstrates analysis of changing neural activity, alongside the paper's broader focus on interpretable prediction from limited labeled electrophysiological data.
neurips-2017-targeting-eeg-lfp-synchrony.tldr: A compact, interpretable neural network learns electrode synchrony features, with a Gaussian process adapter enabling analysis across electrode layouts.

paragraphs: Data recorded across locations and time can contain both temporal correlations and spatial relationships. This paper proposes an additive model that separates these into two components. One captures correlation over time, while the other represents spatial correlation. The separation provides a framework for studying how spatial relationships themselves evolve.

The spatial component uses a time-varying Gaussian graphical model. Its graphical structure represents relationships among spatial variables, and allowing it to change makes evolving patterns part of the model. This directly addresses the goal of estimating spatial structure over time, rather than summarizing the whole recording with a single fixed graph.

Under assumptions that covariance matrices change smoothly, the authors derive strong convergence results from a single sample. Those assumptions are part of the theoretical basis for recovering meaningful evolving structures. They apply the method to human brain fMRI signals to discover time-varying spatial patterns, connecting the statistical model and its guarantees to the analysis of changing brain measurements.
neurips-2017-time-dependent-spatially-va.tldr: An additive space-time model estimates evolving spatial graphs, with single-sample convergence guarantees under covariance-smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: Scientific models often need to predict accurately while identifying a small, understandable set of features. This paper introduces Union of Intersections, or UoI, as a flexible framework for model selection and estimation. It uses intersection operations for selection and union operations for estimation, giving these two tasks distinct roles within a modular approach.

The authors show that UoI can combine low-variance, nearly unbiased estimates of a small feature set with high-quality prediction. These objectives matter together: interpretable feature selection is more useful when estimated effects are stable and predictions remain accurate. The framework is designed to accommodate different modeling tasks rather than only one estimator.

Experiments with UoI Lasso include extracting interpretable functional networks from human electrophysiology and predicting phenotypes using reduced sets of features from genotype-phenotype data. Logistic and matrix-factorization variants also improve predictive parsimony on biomedical benchmarks. The results suggest that the framework could help scientific discovery balance compact explanations with predictive usefulness.
neurips-2017-union-of-intersections-uoi-.tldr: UoI combines intersection-based selection and union-based estimation to support compact, interpretable models with strong predictive performance.

paragraphs: Predicting a system with many agents requires accounting for their interactions. This challenge appears in physical systems, social behavior, and team play. The paper identifies a scaling problem in Interaction Networks: their computational requirements grow with the number of interactions, which is typically quadratic or higher in the number of agents.

The authors introduce VAIN, an attention-based architecture for multi-agent prediction that scales linearly with the number of agents. This changes how computational requirements grow as the system becomes larger. Attention is central to the proposed architecture, providing a different approach to predictive modeling from one whose cost follows the full interaction count.

The method is evaluated on prediction tasks involving chess and soccer, and it outperforms competing multi-agent approaches in those evaluations. These findings support its effectiveness in challenging domains where multiple participants influence the system's behavior. The contribution combines a favorable scaling property with empirical evidence that the architecture remains useful for multi-agent prediction.
neurips-2017-vain-attentional-multi-agen.tldr: VAIN uses attention for multi-agent prediction with linear scaling and outperforms competing approaches on chess and soccer tasks.
